strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a timely and relatively unexplored connection between tokenization, API pricing, and provider incentives. The proposed pay-per-character alternative is simple and potentially useful as a basis for discussion.

Presentation: The principal-agent framing, motivating examples, algorithm, and main empirical findings are generally clear and well organized. Figures are legible, and the manuscript includes concrete token-splitting examples.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers five open-weight models from three families, 400 LMSYS prompts, several temperatures, and multiple top-p values rather than relying on a single model or decoding configuration.
The main top-p hardness construction contains an interesting idea connecting constrained alternative tokenizations to Hamiltonian paths.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly discusses restricted pricing assumptions, prompt representativeness, proprietary models, possible alternative attacks, and the dual-use risk of its overcharging heuristic. It also identifies the hardware, datasets, and model families used.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theorem: Definition 4 requires truthfulness against every reported sequence, including sequences representing different strings. Because generation cost is fixed after t is generated, this definition implies r(t) >= r(t') for every pair; reversing their roles implies that r must be constant over all sequences. Theorem 6 instead characterizes prices invariant only across tokenizations of the same string. Thus the stated incentive-compatibility theorem and the claim that pay-per-character is incentive-compatible are false under the paper's own definition. Restricting deviations to str(t') = str(t) would repair part of the argument, but would establish only retokenization-proofness, not the broader incentive compatibility repeatedly claimed. Moreover, only the necessity direction of Theorem 6 is actually proved.

Soundness—threat and audit model: A provider willing to falsify token counts can also falsify the disclosed next-token distributions, yet the proposed transparency analysis treats those distributions as trustworthy. Conversely, many APIs specify a tokenizer, allowing users to compute the canonical tokenization locally; a systematically different claimed token count would itself raise suspicion. The manuscript does not specify an enforceable protocol connecting the hidden sampled token sequence, disclosed probabilities, and billed count.

Evidence: “Without raising suspicion” is operationalized solely as membership in each top-p set. This is a weak plausibility criterion and does not establish that users or statistical audits would fail to detect systematically noncanonical, revenue-increasing tokenizations. No user study, detector, distribution-level audit, or comparison with realistic billing checks supports the central wording.

The worst-case NP-hardness result uses an arbitrarily constructed next-token process and does not show hardness for actual transformer models. Its formal treatment of the empty-string EOS token is also problematic: EOS belongs to the vocabulary and preserves the decoded string, so tokenization length can become ill-defined or unbounded unless EOS is explicitly excluded from feasible sequences; a footnote saying EOS does not count does not reconcile this with the definitions and objective.

The Appendix B.1.2 probability-threshold extension appears invalid. Its bound assumes an invalid transition occurs in an n-token sequence, but alternative tokenizations can contain fewer than n tokens; then a factor δ times fewer high-probability factors can exceed the threshold ((1-δ)/n)^n. Hence the claimed converse does not follow.

Experimental support is incomplete. Results maximize over the iteration count on the same prompts used for evaluation, without held-out tuning or correction for selection. Only five seeds are used, and the stated 90% t critical value of 2.015 does not match four degrees of freedom. The paper also provides no measured runtime or monetary-cost analysis to support the claim that the extra model pass is negligible.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code or artifact, exact dependency/model revisions, chat templates, complete generation settings, prompt identifiers, or seed list. Appendix A also duplicates Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct where one entry should apparently be the 1B model, and model naming and license footnotes are inconsistent.

Significance is overstated because pay-per-character only removes rewards for changing token boundaries while preserving the string. It does not ensure truthful character counts, output strings, probability reports, model identity, or quality. Its economic consequences are evaluated only by matching average revenue on this selected sample; variance across languages and modalities, alignment with token-dependent inference costs, and input-token billing are not analyzed.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies an underexplored connection between non-unique token representations, usage-based API billing, and provider incentives. The same-string manipulation threat is intuitive and potentially relevant where generation-token counts cannot be independently audited.

Soundness: Under an appropriately restricted same-string threat model, the observation that token-independent pricing favors longer segmentations is valid, and the characterization of additive, tokenization-invariant prices as character-additive is potentially useful.

Evaluation: The authors test five open-weight models from three families using 400 LMSYS prompts, five repetitions, several temperatures and top-p values, and report uncertainty. The appendix supplies additional curves, hardware details, pseudocode, and concrete tokenization examples.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well structured and readable. The distinction between unrestricted overcharging, plausibility-constrained manipulation, and the proposed pricing response is easy to follow.

Limitations/ethics: The paper openly discusses restricted model assumptions, limited prompt representativeness, proprietary-model generalization, and the dual-use risk of its heuristic. These disclosures are appropriate and should not themselves be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive formal error: Definition 4 requires truthful reporting to dominate every reported sequence, not merely alternative tokenizations of the same string. Applying the definition with any two sequences in both directions implies that their rewards must be equal. Thus only constant rewards are incentive-compatible under the stated definition; with standard additive pricing and the empty sequence, this collapses to zero reward. Theorem 6 and the claim that positive pay-per-character pricing is incentive-compatible are therefore false as written: a provider could report a different, longer string and earn more. Earlier prose informally restricts attention to same-string reports, but that restriction is absent from the central definition and theorem.

Soundness/threat model: Transparency about next-token distributions does not provide auditability against the malicious provider being studied. A provider capable of falsifying token IDs can also falsify probabilities unless distributions are independently reproducible or cryptographically attested. Conversely, many real APIs expose known deterministic tokenizers or usage counters that users can approximately audit. The paper does not establish which deployed systems genuinely permit the proposed undetectable manipulation.

Soundness/significance: The NP-hardness result concerns a worst-case, specially constructed autoregressive distribution and vocabulary. The computational problem and representation of that distribution are not formalized carefully enough, and no connection is demonstrated between the reduction and fixed real LLMs. It therefore provides little support for the practical claim that optimal plausible manipulation is hard for actual providers.

Empirical support: The reported 'financial gain' is only the percentage increase in billed tokens. The paper neither measures the extra forward-pass latency and compute cost nor combines costs with actual API prices, so it does not demonstrate increased profit. A verification pass over a 200–300-token sequence is not self-evidently negligible. The headline approximately 13% result also occurs at high temperature and p=0.99; gains are near zero in several lower-p or lower-temperature settings.

Evaluation methodology: The number of heuristic iterations is selected from performance curves on the same 400 prompts, without a held-out selection protocol or an online policy. Only the first 400 filtered LMSYS prompts and artificially bounded 200–300-token generations are used. There are no comparisons with alternative search heuristics, proprietary APIs, common production decoding configurations, multilingual prompts, or shorter typical responses.

Statistical reporting is questionable: with five independent repetitions, a two-sided 90% confidence interval for a mean normally uses four degrees of freedom and a critical value around 2.132, not the stated 2.015. The paper also does not clearly separate variation across prompts from variation across seeds.

Significance/limitations: Pay-per-character merely removes incentives to change segmentation while preserving a string. It does not address incentives to generate verbose text, manipulate Unicode normalization or combining characters, or shift costs across languages with different character-level information density. These issues materially weaken the proposed mechanism's claim to be a fair practical replacement.

Reproducibility: No code, generated outputs, exact prompt identifiers, seeds, dependency versions, or implementation of the plausibility test are supplied. Appendix A also duplicates Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct where one entry should apparently be the 1B model, and its Llama-license footnote points to Gemma terms. These errors make exact replication less reliable.

Ethics: Dual-use risk is acknowledged, but the treatment is brief given that the paper supplies an overbilling method. There is no discussion of responsible disclosure, safeguards for releasing an implementation, or privacy handling for prompts drawn from a real-user conversation dataset. Overall, the interesting premise and competent exposition do not compensate for the contradiction invalidating the central incentive-compatibility theorem and the insufficiently validated real-world threat and economic claims.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a timely and underexplored connection between tokenization and the economic incentives of LLM-service providers. Framing token-count manipulation as a principal-agent problem is conceptually useful.

Soundness: The observation that equal per-token pricing rewards longer reported segmentations is correct under the paper's model. The NP-hardness result, heuristic attack, and pricing characterization provide a coherent combination of theoretical and empirical analysis.

Evaluation: Experiments cover five models from three families, 400 LMSYS prompts, multiple top-p and temperature settings, repeated generations, and confidence intervals. They demonstrate that alternative plausible tokenizations are not merely hypothetical, although the effect varies substantially by setting.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Definitions, algorithms, examples, figures, and limitations make the argument accessible.

Ethics: The paper appropriately discusses the dual-use risk of publishing an overcharging heuristic, frames it as a proof of concept, reports dataset/model licenses, and motivates the work through consumer protection.
weaknesses: The central incentive-compatibility theorem is inconsistent with Definition 4. That definition permits any reported sequence, including one representing a different string. It therefore requires every truthful sequence to maximize payment against every other sequence, which essentially forces payment to be constant. Pay-per-character is not incentive-compatible under this definition because a provider can report a longer string. Theorem 6 becomes valid only after restricting deviations to tokenizations with the same decoded string, as Section 2 informally does. This is a central soundness issue because the paper repeatedly makes the broader claim that pay-per-character eliminates incentives to misreport output sequences.

The threat and audit models are insufficiently justified. In many deployed APIs, billing is defined using a named deterministic tokenizer that users can run locally; for proprietary tokenizers, a dishonest provider able to fabricate token counts may also fabricate the disclosed next-token probabilities. Merely requiring probability transparency does not authenticate the reported generation trace. Trusted execution, cryptographic proofs, or a precise contractual/audit model would be needed to establish when the proposed attack is both feasible and undetectable.

The empirical evidence emphasizes favorable, relatively high-randomness settings. The headline approximately 13% result occurs at temperature 1.3 and top-p 0.99, while gains fall to roughly 0.3% for top-p 0.9 in the main experiment. The appendix evaluates temperatures 1.15–1.45 but not common deterministic or temperature-at-most-1 production configurations. This limits the practical significance of the claimed vulnerability.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or artifact link is supplied; exact seeds, software/model revisions, chat templates, stopping criteria, tie-breaking behavior, and token-pair preprocessing are missing. The stated O(m(log m + sigma_max)) complexity also appears to assume an unreported precomputed data structure for finding the max-min-index split.

The character abstraction needs greater care. Modern tokenizers may operate on bytes, and Unicode code points, grapheme clusters, normalization variants, and invisible characters make 'character' pricing ambiguous and potentially manipulable. The assumption that every character is itself in the vocabulary is not generally valid under a natural Unicode interpretation.

There are smaller presentation and quality-control problems, including a duplicated Llama-3.2-3B model in Appendix A where the 1B model appears intended, inconsistent model naming, duplicated references, and overstatement such as claiming overcharging occurs 'without raising suspicion' when plausibility under a provider-reported distribution is not equivalent to trustworthy auditability. Overall, the idea is promising, but the formal claim and deployment model require revision before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies an underexplored economic consequence of non-unique LLM tokenization and gives a useful principal-agent perspective on token-based API pricing.

Soundness: The attack is demonstrated across five open-weight models from three families, multiple temperatures and top-p values, using LMSYS prompts; the paper also measures verification energy rather than assuming it is free.

The pay-per-character prescription is simple and practically interpretable. Given the intended same-string setting, setting the character price using the mean token-to-character ratio does preserve the average modeled profit margin.

Presentation: The main narrative, algorithms, figures, and limitations discussion are generally clear. The paper explicitly acknowledges restricted model assumptions, proprietary-model generalization, market-level effects, verification difficulties, and the dual-use nature of the attack.
Ethics: The possible misuse of Algorithm 2 is identified, and the work's defensive motivation is explained. I found no unresolved ethical issue that independently precludes publication.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Definition 4 quantifies over every reporting policy and every reported sequence, without requiring the report to preserve the generated string. Under that definition, the claimed pay-per-character mechanism is not incentive-compatible: a zero-cost policy can append characters and collect additional revenue. Theorem 6 is therefore false as stated. It could potentially be repaired by explicitly restricting admissible policies to same-string retokenizations, but that restriction is absent from the central definition.

The appendix proves only the necessary direction of Theorem 6: it derives character-linear prices from Proposition 5. It provides no proof of the advertised converse. This missing direction is particularly consequential because the converse fails under Definition 4.

The practical threat model is insufficiently established. For services with a public, contractually specified tokenizer, users can re-tokenize returned text using the canonical encoding; conversely, a provider willing to falsify metering can fabricate counts or probabilities without constructing a plausible alternative generation path. The paper should distinguish these settings and demonstrate that real API contracts actually bill an unrecoverable sampled token sequence.

The phrase “without raising suspicion” is much stronger than the evaluation supports. Plausibility is defined only as every token belonging to the local top-p set. This does not show that a modified sequence has typical joint probability, matches the advertised sampling distribution statistically, or evades repeated-query auditing. Merely reporting next-token probabilities also does not make them verifiable, as the limitations section itself notes.

The NP-hardness result uses an artificially constructed autoregressive distribution but does not formally specify how that distribution is represented as an input, how the desired top-p sets are realized with probabilities and tie-breaking, or the associated input-size/runtime model. The treatment of the empty-string EOS token and the footnote declaring that it does not count toward sequence length are also inconsistent with the earlier V* and len definitions.

The economic experiment models only GPU energy as cost, assumes verification cost is constant, and measures verification of the original generated sequence rather than the longer attacked sequence. Figure 11 covers only lengths 100–500, so it does not justify the general statement that verification cost is independent of length. Operational, hardware, latency, and batching costs are excluded.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code URL is blank; exact code, seeds, sampled prompt identifiers, package versions, model revisions, and preprocessing details are unavailable. Appendix A says experiments use an A100, while Figure 11 and Table 1 say H100. The model list also repeats Llama-3.2-3B instead of naming the 1B model, and the stated t critical value 2.015 is not the correct 90% two-sided value for five runs.

Presentation is polished overall, but several conclusions are overstated relative to the narrow model—for example, claiming that pay-per-character “eliminates” misreporting incentives despite character padding/verbosity and arbitrary billing fraud remaining possible. The paper acknowledges some of these issues only later in the limitations section.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper identifies a novel economic consequence of non-unique tokenizations and connects tokenization, mechanism design, and LLM-service pricing in a thought-provoking way.

Soundness: The NP-hardness reduction for finding a longest top-p-plausible tokenization has a recognizable core argument, and the empirical heuristic is evaluated across multiple model families, nucleus thresholds, and temperatures.
Soundness/significance: The necessary intuition behind character-based pricing is useful: string-preserving retokenization cannot change revenue when prices depend only on character counts.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with explicit definitions, algorithms, proofs, ablations, concrete tokenization examples, and an unusually candid limitations section.

Ethics: The authors acknowledge that the heuristic could facilitate overcharging, frame it as a proof of concept, and discuss mitigations and broader market effects rather than concealing the dual-use risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 4 quantifies over any reporting policy and reported sequence, whereas Theorem 6 only addresses string-preserving retokenizations. As written, pay-per-character is not incentive-compatible: a zero-cost policy can report additional characters and collect more revenue. The intended restriction appears informally in Section 2 but is absent from the central definition, making the stated if-and-only-if theorem false.

Soundness: Appendix B.3 proves only the necessary direction of Theorem 6. It uses Proposition 5 to derive character-linear prices but never proves the claimed converse. A converse would follow under an explicit string-preserving policy class and nonnegative reporting costs, but those conditions and the proof must be stated.

Soundness: Equation 4 treats every successful run of Algorithm 2 as adding exactly m tokens. Algorithm 2 can terminate before m splits when its selected maximum-ID token has one character, so the asserted “if and only if” profitability condition is not valid without an additional assumption or replacement of m by the realized length increase.

Evidential strength: “Without raising suspicion” is operationalized only as membership in the advertised top-p set. The paper provides no user study, audit model, statistical detection analysis, or argument that top-p plausibility is sufficient to avoid suspicion. It also concedes that users cannot verify the provider's advertised distributions or inference process, substantially weakening the transparency narrative.

Practical significance: The manuscript does not establish that real providers bill according to arbitrary realized token paths rather than a documented or canonical tokenizer, nor does it analyze actual API invoices. Under the assumed untrusted meter, a provider can simply falsify usage, so the experiments do not convincingly isolate a practically important vulnerability specific to tokenization.

Evaluation: The profitability calculation models only measured GPU energy. It omits hardware amortization, batching effects, latency and throughput opportunity costs, CPU work, and other serving expenses. Moreover, the claim that verification cost is sequence-length independent is supported only approximately over a narrow 100–500-token regime and conflicts with the expected length dependence of transformer forward computation. Thus the broad claim of financial profitability is insufficiently supported.

Evaluation: The experiments use only 600 filtered LMSYS prompts for the main results, tune the iteration count on the same evaluations used to report gains, emphasize temperature above 1, and study open-weight models rather than deployed proprietary services. The largest reported gains also occur at p=0.99, while gains at p=0.90–0.95 can be small, limiting generality.

Reproducibility/presentation: The claimed code link is blank. Exact library versions, model revisions, prompt identifiers, seeds, and complete selection procedures are missing. Appendix A duplicates the Llama-3.2-3B model name where one instance apparently should be 1B, and its stated A100 setup conflicts with the H100 used for the energy results. These issues impede independent replication. strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a novel economic consequence of non-unique LLM tokenization and connects tokenization, provider incentives, and mechanism design in a timely and potentially useful way.

Soundness: The combination of a principal-agent formulation, a complexity result, a concrete attack heuristic, and experiments creates a coherent research narrative rather than relying on a purely conceptual concern.

Evaluation: Algorithm 2 is tested on five open-weight models from three families, 600 LMSYS prompts, multiple temperatures and top-p values, with repeated runs and confidence intervals. The appendix also reports energy measurements and multilingual effects of pay-per-character pricing.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized and understandable, with helpful algorithms, examples of altered tokenizations, extensive plots, and a clear explanation of the proposed pay-per-character prescription.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion honestly acknowledges the restricted additive-pricing model, lack of proprietary-model evaluation, questionable representativeness of LMSYS prompts, broader market effects, verbosity gaming under character pricing, and the dual-use risk of the attack heuristic.
weaknesses: Soundness: Definition 4 quantifies over any reporting policy and reported sequence, without requiring the report to preserve the generated string. Under that definition, a character-linear mechanism is not incentive-compatible: a zero-cost policy could report a different, longer string for greater revenue. Theorem 6 is therefore false as written unless reporting policies are explicitly restricted to string-preserving retokenizations.

Soundness: The appendix proves only the necessary direction of Theorem 6. It derives character-linear prices from incentive compatibility but does not prove the claimed converse. The converse is straightforward under the missing string-preservation restriction, but the current theorem and proof do not establish the paper's central guarantee.

Practical significance: The threat model is insufficiently grounded in actual API accounting. For models with public tokenizers, users can generally recompute a canonical token count from returned text; for opaque providers, a malicious provider can simply falsify usage counts or probability reports. The paper does not establish when users are billed according to the hidden sampled segmentation, provide evidence of a deployed API vulnerable in this precise manner, or supply a trusted way to verify the claimed next-token distributions.

Theory: The top-p hardness reduction specifies desired nucleus sets but does not rigorously construct probability distributions with polynomially representable probabilities whose smallest cumulative-probability sets equal those sets, particularly for a fixed p and varying set sizes. Thus the stated NP-hardness result needs a more careful realizability argument. Moreover, worst-case hardness alone provides limited support for claims about real provider behavior.

Evaluation: Equation 4 treats every successful run as adding exactly m tokens and assumes a length-independent verification cost, although Algorithm 2 can terminate before m splits and transformer verification normally depends on sequence length and implementation. The empirical constant-cost observation is narrow and should not be generalized without latency, batching, hardware utilization, and non-energy operating costs.

Reproducibility: The promised code URL is blank. The appendix also conflicts on hardware—A100s in the setup versus an H100 in Figure 11 and Table 1—and repeats Llama-3.2-3B in the model list where one entry appears intended to be 1B. Library versions, exact seeds, preprocessing details, and implementation specifics are incomplete.

Evaluation methodology: The same prompt collection appears to be used to choose the optimal iteration count m and report its benefit, with no held-out evaluation. Only five repetitions are used, and there is no comparison against stronger search methods or straightforward auditing baselines. These issues weaken the quantitative claims of profitable, difficult-to-detect overcharging.

Presentation: Several strong phrases, including that users can be overcharged 'without raising suspicion' and that the heuristic is financially profitable, overreach the evidence because plausibility under top-p is only a limited proxy for detectability and the cost analysis covers GPU energy rather than total provider cost.
